area: Area III. Airspace and VFR Rules
objective: By the end of this lesson you can state the dimensions, entry, pilot certificate, radio, transponder and ADS-B Out rules for Class A, B, C, D, E and G airspace, and plan a route through several classes knowing exactly what each one needs.
why: Each class has its own entry, radio and equipment rules. Get one wrong, like entering Class B on flight following alone or flying a failed ADS-B Out into a Mode C veil, and you are somewhere ATC and other pilots don't expect you.

warmup: You call approach 15 NM from a Class C airport and hear: "Aircraft calling approach, standby." Can you enter the Class C? What exactly would have to be different for the answer to be yes?

key_terms.def: Class A, B, C, D and E airspace, where ATC serves IFR flights, and VFR flights as the class requires.
The airport a Class B, C or D area is designated for. Any other airport inside is a satellite airport.
ATC answered your call using your call sign. "N123AB, standby" counts.
Within 30 NM of an Appendix D, section 1 airport, surface to 10,000 ft MSL. Transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out required.
Uncharted area, normally out to 20 NM, where Class C services are offered. Participation is voluntary.
Avionics that broadcast the aircraft's GNSS position and other data about once per second to ATC and other aircraft.
ADS-B Out on 1090 MHz, built into a transponder. The only kind allowed in Class A.
ADS-B on 978 MHz. Meets the ADS-B Out rule only below 18,000 ft MSL.
Class E starting at 700 ft AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 ft AGL (blue vignette).
A Class C or D surface area that becomes Class E or G when the tower closes. The Chart Supplement says which.

chunks.title: The big picture: classes and overlaps

body.p: Airspace is either regulatory (Class A, B, C, D and E, plus restricted and prohibited areas) or nonregulatory (MOAs, warning, alert and controlled firing areas, and national security areas) [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]]. Controlled airspace means Classes A to E: ATC serves IFR flights there, and VFR flights as the class requires [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1a]]. Class G is whatever is not A, B, C, D or E [[33:189|AIM 3-3-1]].

head: Class
Generally
On the VFR chart
rows: 18,000 ft MSL up to and including FL 600, including the waters within 12 NM of the coast of the 48 states and Alaska [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]
Surface to 10,000 ft MSL around the busiest airports; a surface area and two or more layers [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3a]]
Solid blue lines; ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]
Surface to 4,000 ft above the airport (charted MSL); usually a 5 NM core and a 10 NM shelf no lower than 1,200 ft [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]]
Solid magenta lines; ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]
Surface to 2,500 ft above the airport (charted MSL), around airports with an operating tower [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5a]]
Blue dashed line; ceiling in a box, in hundreds of feet MSL [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]
All other controlled airspace: surface areas, 700 or 1,200 ft AGL transition areas, airways, 14,500 ft MSL up to 18,000 ft, and above FL 600 [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6d]] [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]]
Magenta dashed line (surface area); magenta or blue vignettes for 700 or 1,200 ft floors [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]]
Surface up to the base of the overlying Class E [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]]
Not outlined. It is what is left below the Class E floors [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]]

callout.text: Overlap rule: the more restrictive class's rules apply. A beats B, B beats C, C beats D, D beats E, E beats G [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].

check.q: A Class B shelf sits over Class E airspace. Whose rules apply in the Class B?
check.a: Class B's. Where designations overlap, the more restrictive one applies [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].

body.p: Class A (91.135): fly IFR, under an ATC clearance received before you enter, with a two-way radio and two-way communication with ATC the whole time. The aircraft needs the 91.215 transponder and the 91.225 ADS-B Out [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]]. Because IFR is required, the PIC needs an instrument rating [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "any ADS-B Out works in Class A." Class A needs 1090 MHz extended squitter (1090ES) equipment, TSO-C166b or C166c [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]]. A 978 MHz UAT meets the rule only below 18,000 ft MSL [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(b)]] [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a4]].

body.p: Class E is the controlled airspace that isn't A, B, C or D [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]]. Its common forms [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]]:

bullets: Surface areas at airports without an operating tower. The airport needs weather reporting and radio coverage down to the runway [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6e1]].
Extensions to surface areas that contain instrument approaches, with no radio requirement for VFR pilots [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].
Transition areas from 700 ft AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 ft AGL (blue vignette). They stay in effect all the time, whatever the airport's hours [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].
Federal airways and T-routes: 1,200 ft AGL up to, but not including, 18,000 ft MSL, unless otherwise specified [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].
Everywhere from 14,500 ft MSL up to 18,000 ft (but not within 1,500 ft of the surface), and everything above FL 600 [[60:416|14 CFR 71.71(a)]].

body.p: Entry: no pilot certificate and no VFR radio requirement [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6b]]. Equipment: a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out at and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states and DC, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6b]]. Near an airport in a Class E area, follow the Class G rules of 91.126 and any part 93 traffic patterns [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127]].

callout.text: When a part-time tower closes, its Chart Supplement entry says "other times CLASS E" or "other times CLASS G" [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].

check.q: You fly VFR at 8,500 ft MSL in Class E with no radio. Legal as far as the airspace goes?
check.a: Yes. VFR in Class E has no certificate, radio or entry requirement [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6b]]. Weather minimums and the airspace along the rest of the route still apply.

chunks.title: Class G, and towers outside Class B, C and D

body.p: Class G (uncontrolled) runs from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E. ATC has no authority or responsibility to control traffic there, but VFR weather minimums still apply [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]]. No pilot certificate, radio or equipment requirement [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]].
Arriving at a nontowered airport in Class G, airplanes make all turns to the left, unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

callout.text: 91.126(d) and 91.127(c): no one may operate to, from, through or on an airport with an operating control tower without two-way radio contact with the tower. Establish it before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127]].

Common mistake: "a tower always means Class D." Some towered airports sit in Class G airspace (the PHAK names Lake City, FL). Check the Chart Supplement, formerly the Airport/Facility Directory [[1:386|PHAK 15-11]].

body.p: Radio fails in flight under VFR? You may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower and you receive a clearance to land [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]]. With no radio, that clearance is a steady green light [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

check.q: You pass 2 NM from a towered airport in Class G at 3,500 ft AGL. Must you talk to the tower?
check.a: No. The tower contact rule applies before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL; you are above that [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]].

body.p: Class D generally runs from the surface to 2,500 ft above the airport elevation, charted in MSL, around airports with an operating tower. Each one is tailored and normally contains its instrument procedures [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5a]].

bullets: Pilot certificate: none specific. Equipment: a two-way radio, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5b]].
Arriving or passing through: establish two-way radio communications with the ATC facility before you enter, and keep them while inside [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]].
Departing the primary airport or a towered satellite: talk to the tower. From a nontowered satellite: call the Class D facility as soon as practicable after departing [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(2)]].
At a towered airport, operating on a runway or taxiway, taking off and landing all need an ATC clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.129(i)]].
Radio failure under VFR: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower and you get a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]].

callout.text: On the chart: blue dashed line and a boxed ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL. A minus in front, like -27, means up to but not including 2,700 ft [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]] [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

body.p: Part-time towers: when the tower is closed, the surface area becomes Class E or Class G, as the Chart Supplement states. If it becomes Class G, it is Class G up to the overlying controlled airspace, normally the 700 or 1,200 ft AGL Class E [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5a2]]. Arrival extensions: if any one is longer than 2 NM, all of them are Class E [[33:187|AIM 3-2-5d]]. ATC gives VFR aircraft no separation in Class D [[33:187|AIM 3-2-5e]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "if the controller answered, I'm in." Only a reply with your call sign establishes communication. "N123AB, standby" means you may enter. "Aircraft calling Manassas tower, standby" does not, and "remain outside the Class Delta" means stay out [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5b]].

check.q: The tower closed at 2200 and the Chart Supplement says "other times CLASS G." At 2300, what is the airspace 500 ft over the runway?
check.a: Class G, up to the overlying controlled airspace, normally Class E at 700 or 1,200 ft AGL [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5a2]].

body.p: Class C surrounds airports with an operating tower, a radar approach control and enough IFR traffic or passengers. It usually has a 5 NM core from the surface to 4,000 ft above the airport, and a 10 NM shelf from no lower than 1,200 ft up to 4,000 ft above the airport, all charted in MSL [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]].

bullets: Pilot certificate: none specific [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c]].

Arriving or passing through: establish two-way radio communications before entering and keep them inside. Departing: the tower, or from a nontowered satellite, the Class C facility as soon as practicable [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]].
Equipment: two-way radio, plus the 91.215 transponder with altitude reporting and the 91.225 ADS-B Out [[60:455|14 CFR 91.130(d)]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c]].
Above it: transponder and ADS-B Out are also required above the ceiling and within the lateral limits, up to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]].
Satellite airports inside: take off and land using the FAA arrival and departure traffic patterns [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(b)]].

body.p: Call far enough out that you can't enter before contact is made. Give your position, altitude, beacon code and destination, and request Class C service [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]. Chart notes say to contact approach generally within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]. The uncharted outer area normally reaches 20 NM [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "Class C needs a clearance." It doesn't. It needs two-way radio communications established before entry [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(1)]], which means ATC answered with your call sign [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]. A radar outage doesn't remove that requirement [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18f NOTE]].

A Class C ceiling charted as T means up to, but not including, the floor of the Class B above [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]. Some Class C areas offer services only part-time; outside those hours, the radio and equipment rules follow the class then in effect [[33:183|AIM 3-2-4e NOTE 3]].

check.q: You plan to fly over a Class C at 6,500 ft MSL. Its ceiling is 4,800 ft MSL. Is ADS-B Out required?
check.a: Yes. Above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class C, up to 10,000 ft MSL, transponder and ADS-B Out are required [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]]. No radio contact is needed, since you are outside the Class C.

body.p: Class B surrounds the busiest airports, generally from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL. It is tailored into a surface area and two or more layers, like an upside-down wedding cake [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3a]].

head: Requirement
What the rule says
rows: An ATC clearance from the facility with jurisdiction before you operate in the area, whatever the weather [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]] [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3b]]
At least a private certificate; or a recreational, sport or student pilot who has met the part 61 training and endorsement rules named in 91.131 [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]]
Takeoff and landing need at least a private certificate. No solo student, sport or recreational pilots [[60:650|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 4]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]]
Operable two-way radio for everyone. For IFR, an operable VOR or TACAN receiver or a suitable RNAV system [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(c)]]
Transponder with automatic altitude reporting (91.215(a)) and ADS-B Out (91.225) [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(d)]]

body.p: On the chart, each sector shows ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL, in blue. A floor with a + means "from above": at and below that altitude you are outside the Class B [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]. Arriving VFR, call ATC relative to the charted points, even while still under the floor [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]]. Transiting, ATC may clear you when traffic permits. Otherwise fly above or below it, or use a VFR corridor (122.750 MHz for position reports there) [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "I'm on flight following, so I can go in." Class B needs a clearance [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]], and you keep that responsibility while receiving radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1d]]. A radar outage doesn't remove it either [[33:220|AIM 4-1-18f NOTE]].

body.p: Inside, VFR pilots get sequencing and separation. ATC may assign altitudes that don't match 91.159; when you hear "resume appropriate VFR altitudes," go back to a 91.159 altitude [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e]]. Outside, stay well clear of the boundaries, especially where a floor is 3,000 ft AGL or less [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3f]].

check.q: A sector is charted 70 over +40. You are at 4,000 ft MSL. Inside or outside the Class B?
check.a: Outside. A + floor means upward from above 4,000 ft; at and below it you are outside [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

chunks.title: Transponder and ADS-B Out: where they're required

body.p: 91.215(b) (transponder with Mode C altitude reporting) and 91.225 (ADS-B Out) cover almost the same airspace [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]:

head: Airspace
Transponder + altitude (91.215)
ADS-B Out (91.225)
rows: Mode C veil: within 30 NM of an Appendix D, section 1 airport, surface to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:647|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 1]]
Above a Class B or C ceiling, within its lateral limits, up to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]]
At and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states and DC, except at and below 2,500 ft AGL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]
Class E at and above 3,000 ft MSL over the Gulf, from the coastline out to 12 NM [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(5)]] [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f]]
Class D, Class G, and Class E below 10,000 ft MSL outside all of the above [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f]]

body.p: Exception: aircraft not originally certificated with an engine-driven electrical system (and not since certified with one), balloons and gliders may skip the 10,000 ft rule. They may fly in the Mode C veil if they stay outside Class A, B and C and below the Class B or C ceiling or 10,000 ft MSL, whichever is lower [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(3)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(e)]].

ADS-B Out gets your position from GNSS and broadcasts it about once per second [[33:300|AIM 4-5-7a1]], on 1090 MHz (1090ES, built into a transponder) or 978 MHz (UAT) [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a2]]. Below 18,000 ft either one works; Class A needs 1090ES. ADS-B In (traffic and weather on board) is not required [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a4]].

callout.text: Use: with an operable transponder, keep it on, with Mode C, in all 91.215(b) airspace and all controlled airspace [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. ADS-B Out must transmit at all times unless ATC directs otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(f)]]. VFR code is 1200 unless ATC assigns one [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20a5]]. On the airport movement area, keep altitude reporting and ADS-B on [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20a3]].

Common mistake: "there's a 10 NM transponder ring around some airports." 91.215(b)(5)(ii) still exists, but its airport list, Appendix D, section 2, is reserved: no airports are on it [[60:648|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 2]].

Changed: the current AIM calls it the Gulf of America, while 91.225(d)(5) still says Gulf of Mexico. Same airspace: Class E at and above 3,000 ft MSL out to 12 NM. It needs ADS-B Out but not a transponder [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6b]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(5)]].

check.q: You are 25 NM from an Appendix D, section 1 airport at 2,500 ft MSL, outside its Class B. Are a transponder and ADS-B Out required?
check.a: Yes. That is the Mode C veil: within 30 NM, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]].

head: Situation
When to ask ATC
rows: Transponder works, but no Mode C altitude reporting
Transponder inoperative: to the destination (with stops) or to a repair place
ADS-B Out inoperative: to the destination (with stops) or to a repair place
At least 1 hour before [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]]. The AIM says to use the FAA's web authorization tool, 1 to 24 hours before [[33:180|AIM 3-2-3b5 NOTE]]
In writing at least 4 days before. ATC may approve an inoperative transponder right away to continue to the destination or a repair place [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(d)]]

body.p: Requests go to the ATC facility with jurisdiction over the airspace [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]]. Without the equipment or an authorization, fly only outside ADS-B airspace [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7d4]].

callout.text: If ATC gives a non-equipped airplane a heading, route or altitude into ADS-B airspace, comply but say you are "negative ADS-B equipment" with no authorization. The FAA normally won't take enforcement action when ATC started the change. Don't request one yourself except for safety, such as weather [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7d4]].

body.p: ATC may tell you, "Your ADS-B transmitter appears to be inoperative or malfunctioning. Stop ADS-B transmissions" [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7d3]]. Make sure your ADS-B flight ID matches the aircraft ID in your flight plan, or ATC may not link you to it [[33:302|AIM 4-5-7c2]] [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7d1]].

check.q: Your ADS-B Out fails at a fuel stop inside a Mode C veil. Can you fly home?
check.a: Ask the ATC facility with jurisdiction for an authorization to fly to your destination or a repair place. For an inoperative unit, that request may be made any time [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: plan a route through several classes

body.p: Use a current sectional or TAC, the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs. For each part of the route, name the class and what it needs [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]]:

bullets: 1. Draw the line and list every airspace it touches, including floors, ceilings, shelves and the 30 NM Mode C veil ring [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].
2. Where two classes overlap, use the more restrictive one's rules [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].
3. Check part-time airspace and services in the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]] [[33:184|AIM 3-2-4g]].
4. For each class, confirm certificate and entry: A, IFR clearance; B, clearance; C and D, two-way contact; E and G, none for VFR [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]].
5. Check the airplane: Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out working for B, C, the veil, above B and C, and 10,000 ft MSL and up [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f]].

6. Write down frequencies and call points: Class C approach about 20 NM out, Class B reporting points, Class D tower before the boundary [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]] [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5b]].
7. Plan your way around: an altitude or route that stays out of the Class B if no clearance comes [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]].

callout.text: Common mistake: using PHAK Figure 15-9 as the whole story. It lists the transponder but shows ADS-B Out only in a footnote, and its Class B note leaves out sport pilots [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]]. The current rules are 91.130(d), 91.131(b) and (d), and 91.225 [[60:455|14 CFR 91.130(d)]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(d)]].

check.q: Your route: Class G departure, then under a Class B shelf inside the Mode C veil, then a Class D. What does the under-the-shelf leg need?
check.a: No clearance, since you stay below the floor, but an operating Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out, since you are in the veil [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]].

chunks.title: Risk: entering Class B or C without clearance or contact

body.p: Meeting the Class B clearance and the Class C and D radio rules before entry is your job, not ATC's, and it stays your job while you receive radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1d]].

head: Hazard
What protects you
rows: Hearing what you expect: "standby" without your call sign
Communication isn't established; you may not enter [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]
ATC may tell you to remain outside until it can provide service; stay out [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]
Call far enough out that you can't enter before contact [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5b]]
Flight following mistaken for a Class B clearance
Only an ATC clearance lets you in [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]] [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1d]]
Flying right at a Class B floor or boundary
Stay clear of the edges, especially floors 3,000 ft AGL or lower [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3f]]

body.p: Brief it before takeoff: the frequency, where you will call, and where you will wait outside. Plan an altitude under the floor or a route around [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]]. Once inside, if an assigned heading or altitude would put you in a cloud, too near terrain or into wake, tell ATC and get a revised clearance [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e]].

callout.text: Class B: hear a clearance. Class C or D: hear your call sign. Neither? Stay out [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]] [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(1)]] [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]].

check.q: Approach answers, "N123AB, remain outside the Class Charlie airspace and standby." May you enter?
check.a: No. Contact is established, but you have been told to remain outside until conditions permit [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]].

f1.caption: Figure 16-2. VFR Terminal Area Chart and legend.
f1.alt: New Orleans VFR Terminal Area Chart excerpt. Blue Class B sectors around Louis Armstrong New Orleans International (MSY) are labeled with ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet, such as 70 over SFC, 70 over 20, 70 over 10 and 70 over 40, with notes excluding the airspace below 600 ft MSL. Blue dashed Class D circles with boxed 25 ceilings surround Lakefront and New Orleans NAS JRB. A purple hatched alert area boundary crosses the chart, and the chart legend panels are on the right.

f2.caption: FIG 3-2-1. Airspace Classes.
f2.alt: U.S. airspace classes at a glance: Class A in red from 18,000 ft MSL to FL 600, Class E above FL 600 and from 14,500 ft MSL, an upside-down wedding cake for Class B, a two-tier Class C, a cylinder for Class D, and Class G near the surface with floors at 700 and 1,200 ft AGL around nontowered airports.

f3.caption: Figure 15-9. Requirements for airspace operations.
f3.alt: Table of entry requirements, equipment and minimum pilot certificate for Class A, B, C, D, E and G. Class A: ATC clearance, IFR equipped, instrument rating. Class B: ATC clearance, two-way radio and transponder with altitude reporting, private (with student and recreational exceptions). Class C: two-way radio communications before entry, two-way radio and transponder. Class D: two-way radio communications before entry, two-way radio. Class E and G: no specific requirements for VFR. A footnote says ADS-B Out may be required under 91.225.

f4.caption: FIG 4-5-6. ADS-B, TIS-B, and FIS-B: Broadcast Services Architecture.
f4.alt: Two airplanes broadcasting ADS-B on UAT and/or 1090 to each other and to ground radio stations. Ground stations send ADS-B, ADS-R, TIS-B and FIS-B through a ground broadcast server inside the control facilities, which also links to radar sites, TIS-B surveillance processing, FIS sources and ATC automation. Notes: no FIS-B over 1090 links; both aircraft must be on the same link for direct ADS-B.

f5.caption: Airspace Information (Continued): Class C, Class D and Class E Airspace.
f5.alt: Sectional symbols: a magenta Class C arc with 48 over 30 for ceiling and floor and a CTC approach box; blue dashed Class D circles with boxed 27 and -27 ceilings and a Class D exclusion below 1,500 ft MSL; magenta dashed Class E surface areas; magenta vignette for a 700 ft AGL Class E floor, blue vignette for a 1,200 ft AGL floor next to Class G, and a ceiling symbol of 14,000 ft MSL.

scenario.title: Lunch at a Class B primary airport
scenario.setup: You hold a private certificate and fly a Cessna 182 with a Mode C transponder and 1090ES ADS-B Out. You plan a VFR trip from a nontowered Class G airport to the primary airport of a nearby Class B (not one of the Appendix D, section 4 airports) with a friend who holds a sport pilot certificate. The approach frequency is busy.

questions.q: Before you leave, what do the rules require for you to land at the Class B primary airport?
questions.a: A private certificate (you have it), an ATC clearance before entering the Class B, an operable two-way radio, and the transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(c)]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(d)]].

questions.q: Approach says "radar contact" and gives you a squawk code, but no clearance. The boundary is 2 NM ahead. What do you do?
questions.a: Stay out. You need an ATC clearance to enter Class B [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]], and radar service doesn't change your responsibility [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1d]]. Turn or hold outside and ask for the clearance.

questions.q: You're cleared in and assigned 3,500 ft, which isn't a VFR cruising altitude. Later ATC says "resume appropriate VFR altitudes." What does each mean?
questions.a: ATC may assign VFR altitudes that don't conform to 91.159 in Class B. "Resume appropriate VFR altitudes" means return to a 91.159 altitude [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e]].

questions.q: An assigned heading would take you into a cloud. What do you do?
questions.a: Tell approach and get a revised clearance or instruction. Class B service doesn't relieve you of VFR weather minimums [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e]].

questions.q: Your friend asks whether he could fly solo into this airport as a sport pilot. What's the rule?
questions.a: A sport pilot may operate in Class B and at its airports after meeting 61.325, except at the Appendix D, section 4 airports, which need at least a private certificate [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]] [[60:650|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 4]].

skills.do: Given a VFR route on a sectional or TAC that crosses Class G, E, D, C and B airspace and a Mode C veil, name each class with its floor and ceiling, and state what each needs: pilot certificate, clearance or two-way contact, radio, transponder and ADS-B Out, plus frequencies and call points.
skills.practice: Plan a local trip across your area's Class B or C and walk it with your CFI using the step-by-step list above. Check each leg against 91.129 to 91.135 [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]], the transponder and ADS-B tables in AIM 4-1-20 [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20f]], and the chart symbols [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

quiz.q: What do you need before entering Class C airspace VFR?
options: An ATC clearance
A filed VFR flight plan
Two-way radio communications established
At least a private pilot certificate
quiz.why: Class C requires two-way radio communications with ATC established before entry, not a clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(1)]]. No specific certificate is required [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c]].

quiz.q: Where two airspace designations overlap, which rules apply?
options: The less restrictive designation's
The more restrictive designation's
Whichever one is charted on top
The one with the lower floor
quiz.why: The operating rules of the more restrictive designation apply [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].

options: From the surface to 2,500 ft above the airport elevation
From the surface to 4,000 ft above the airport elevation
From the surface to 10,000 ft MSL
From 700 ft AGL to 2,500 ft AGL
quiz.why: Class D generally runs from the surface to 2,500 ft above the airport elevation, charted in MSL [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5a]]. 4,000 ft is the usual Class C height [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]].

quiz.q: Which ADS-B Out equipment meets the rule in Class A?
options: Either 978 MHz UAT or 1090ES
978 MHz UAT only
Any Mode S transponder, with no ADS-B
1090 MHz extended squitter (1090ES)
quiz.why: Class A needs equipment meeting TSO-C166b or C166c, which is 1090ES [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]] [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a4]]. UAT meets the rule only below 18,000 ft MSL [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(b)]].

options: Within 30 NM of an Appendix D, section 1 airport, surface to 10,000 ft MSL
Within 10 NM of any Class C airport, up to 4,000 ft AGL
Within 20 NM of a Class B airport, up to 12,500 ft MSL
The Class B surface area only
quiz.why: 91.215(b)(2) and 91.225(d)(2) cover all airspace within 30 NM of the Appendix D, section 1 airports, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]].

quiz.q: At the 12 airports in Appendix D, section 4, who may not take off or land solo?
options: A private pilot
A commercial pilot
A student pilot with the 61.95 endorsements
An airline transport pilot
quiz.why: Solo student, sport and recreational pilot operations are not permitted at those airports; at least a private certificate is required [[60:650|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 4]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]].

quiz.q: On a sectional, a Class C ceiling shown as T means:
options: Tower hours only
Up to, but not including, the floor of the overlying Class B
A terrain-based ceiling given in AGL
Temporary airspace; check NOTAMs
quiz.why: A T ceiling means the Class C goes up to, but not including, the floor of the Class B above [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

quiz.q: Your airplane has no transponder. How early must you ask ATC to operate where 91.215(b) requires one?
options: Any time
At least 4 days before, in writing
At least 24 hours before
At least 1 hour before
quiz.why: For an aircraft not equipped with a transponder, the request must be made at least one hour before the operation [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)-(3)]]. "Any time" is for an inoperative transponder or a missing Mode C [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(d)(1)]].

quiz.q: Unless otherwise specified, Class E federal airways extend from:
options: 1,200 ft AGL up to, but not including, 18,000 ft MSL
700 ft AGL to 14,500 ft MSL
The surface to 18,000 ft MSL
1,500 ft AGL to FL 600
quiz.why: Federal airways and low-altitude RNAV routes are Class E from 1,200 ft AGL up to, but not including, 18,000 ft MSL, unless otherwise specified [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].

takeaways: Class B: hear a clearance. Class C and D: hear your call sign. Class A: IFR under a clearance.
Where airspace overlaps, the more restrictive class's rules apply.
Transponder and ADS-B Out: Class A, B and C, the 30 NM veil, above B and C up to 10,000 ft, and 10,000 ft MSL and up except within 2,500 ft of the ground.
Class A needs 1090ES. A UAT works only below 18,000 ft MSL.
Broken transponder or ADS-B: ask ATC any time. Not installed: at least 1 hour before. Class A: in writing 4 days before.
Radar advisories never replace a Class B clearance. Always plan where you'll wait outside.
cfi_notes: PHAK 15-10 says no pilot may take off or land at a satellite airport in Class D except by the FAA arrival and departure patterns. That paragraph is 91.130(b) for Class C; current 91.129 has no such line. Teach from 91.129 [[60:452|14 CFR 91.129]] [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(b)]].

PHAK Figure 15-9 shows ADS-B Out only as a footnote ("may be required") and its Class B note mentions only student and recreational pilots. Teach 91.131(b), 91.130(d) and 91.225 instead [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]].

PHAK 15-10 and 15-11 say to contact the tower "within" 4 NM. The regulation says communications must be established "prior to 4 nautical miles" from the airport. Teach the regulation's wording [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[1:385|PHAK 15-10]].

91.215(b)(5)(i) applies to all airspace at and above 10,000 ft MSL (except at and below 2,500 ft AGL), while 91.225(d)(4) says Class E airspace. Students quoting one as the other are usually right in practice, but know the difference [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

Examiners commonly probe the "standby" notes: with call sign, without call sign, and "remain outside." Role-play the Class C and D calls until the student answers without hesitation [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]].

Some pilots remember a 10 NM transponder ring around certain airports. The paragraph is still in 91.215(b)(5)(ii), but Appendix D, section 2 lists no airports [[60:648|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 2]].

For an aircraft with no ADS-B Out, 91.225(g)(2) sets the minimum (at least 1 hour before); the AIM adds the method (the FAA web tool, 1 to 24 hours before). Teach both [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]] [[33:180|AIM 3-2-3b5 NOTE]].
Keep this lesson on entry and equipment. VFR weather minimums and special VFR are RF.III.B, special use airspace and TFRs are RF.III.C, and speed limits are RF.III.D.
gaps: The sources don't list current Class B, C and D areas or their dimensions (FAA Order JO 7400.11 isn't included). Pilots must use current charts, the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs.
AC 90-114 (ADS-B operations) and the FAA's ADS-B deviation web tool are named in the AIM but are not in the source set.
Operating a specific transponder or ADS-B unit (controls, anonymous mode, failure messages) comes from the POH or AFM supplement, not these sources.
No source has a common-errors list for airspace; the common mistakes in this lesson come from the regulation and AIM text.

activities.title: True or false: Class A, E and G
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Class A airspace is drawn on sectional charts.
cards.why: No. Class A is not specifically charted, and visual charts don't depict it [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]] [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

cards.s: Class E transition areas starting at 700 or 1,200 ft AGL stay in effect even when the nearby tower is closed.
cards.why: Yes. They remain in effect continuously, regardless of airport hours or surface area status [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].

cards.s: Where no lower Class E base is charted, Class E begins at 14,500 ft MSL.
cards.why: Yes. Where charts show no Class E base, Class E begins at 14,500 ft MSL [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].

cards.s: A 978 MHz UAT meets the ADS-B Out rule at FL 200.
cards.why: No. FL 200 is Class A, which needs 1090ES (TSO-C166b or C166c) [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]]. UAT is allowed only below 18,000 ft MSL [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7a4]].

cards.s: At a towered airport in Class G, you must reach the tower before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL.
cards.why: Yes. 91.126(d) applies at any airport with an operating control tower [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]].

cards.s: Class G has no VFR weather minimums, because ATC doesn't control it.
cards.why: No. ATC has no control authority there, but VFR minimums still apply [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].

cards.s: Arriving at a nontowered Class G airport with no light signals or markings, make right turns in the pattern.
cards.why: No. Make all turns to the left unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]].

activities.title: What did ATC just tell you?
activities.intro: Tap a radio call or situation, then what it means for entering the airspace.

pairs.r: Contact established; you may enter Class C or D
Not established; you may not enter
Stay outside until ATC can take you

pairs.l: Class C approach radar is out
pairs.r: Two-way radio contact is still required to enter
Class G up to the overlying Class E

activities.title: Read the New Orleans TAC
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Class B surface area, SFC to 7,000 MSL

activities.title: Transponder, ADS-B Out, both or neither?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: 20 NM from an App. D sec. 1 airport, 3,000 ft, outside the Class B
Over a Class C, within its lateral limits, at 7,500 ft MSL
12,500 ft MSL over flat terrain at 1,000 ft MSL
Class E over the Gulf at 4,500 ft MSL, 6 NM offshore, far from Class B and C
Class D surface area far from any Class B or C
11,500 ft MSL over a ridge at 9,500 ft MSL, far from Class B and C
Class G at 1,000 ft AGL, far from any Class B or C

activities.title: Work out the airspace numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A Class D airport's elevation is 800 ft MSL. Its Class D goes up to 2,500 ft above the airport. What ceiling, in feet MSL, will be charted?
items.why: 800 + 2,500 = 3,300 ft MSL, charted in hundreds of feet MSL as a boxed 33 [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5a]] [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

items.q: A Class C primary airport sits at 1,200 ft MSL, with the usual ceiling of 4,000 ft above the airport. What is the ceiling in feet MSL?
items.why: 1,200 + 4,000 = 5,200 ft MSL. Class C goes up to 4,000 ft above the airport elevation, charted in MSL [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]].

items.q: You cruise at 10,500 ft MSL, outside Class B and C, over a ridge at 8,200 ft MSL. How high above the ground are you?
items.why: 10,500 - 8,200 = 2,300 ft AGL. That is at or below 2,500 ft AGL, so the 10,000 ft MSL transponder and ADS-B Out rule doesn't apply there [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

items.q: A towered airport in Class G is at 1,350 ft MSL. Up to what altitude, in feet MSL, does the tower contact rule reach near the field?
items.why: The rule reaches up to and including 2,500 ft AGL: 1,350 + 2,500 = 3,850 ft MSL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]].

items.q: A Class C chart note says to contact approach within 20 NM. At 120 knots groundspeed, how many minutes do you have from 20 NM until you reach the 10 NM shelf edge?
items.why: 20 - 10 = 10 NM. 120 knots is 2 NM per minute, so 10 / 2 = 5 minutes [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]]. Contact must be established before you enter [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(1)]].

activities.title: Can I legally and safely fly this?
activities.intro: You rent N123AB, a Cessna 172 with a Mode C transponder and a 978 MHz UAT ADS-B Out. You hold a private certificate. Today: VFR from a nontowered Class G field, past a Class B, through a Class C to a Class D airport for lunch, then home.

steps.s: Planning: your route passes 18 NM from the Class B primary airport (an Appendix D, section 1 airport) at 3,500 ft MSL, below the Class B shelf. What does this leg need?
options: Nothing; you stay below the Class B floor
A Class B clearance before you reach the 30 NM ring
An operating Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out, because you're inside the Mode C veil
A call to the primary airport's tower
steps.why: Within 30 NM of an Appendix D, section 1 airport, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL, you need a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]]. Under the floor you are not yet in the Class B, so no clearance is needed there [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3d2]].

steps.s: Runup: the ADS-B Out shows a failure message. Everything else works. What's your best move?
options: Go; the transponder alone is enough in the veil
Fix it before flying into ADS-B airspace, or ask ATC for an authorization first
Turn the ADS-B unit off so ATC won't see the fault
Go, and squawk 7600 when you reach the veil
steps.why: The veil, Class B and Class C all need ADS-B Out [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]. For an inoperative unit you may ask the ATC facility with jurisdiction for an authorization any time [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]]; otherwise stay outside ADS-B airspace [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7d4]].

steps.s: A mechanic fixes it and it tests good. Airborne, 12 NM from the Class C, you call approach and hear: "Aircraft calling approach, standby." What now?
options: Continue in; ATC answered you
Stay outside the Class C and call again
Descend below 1,200 ft AGL and fly under the shelf to the core
Squawk 1200 and enter, since you're VFR
steps.why: A reply without your call sign means communication is not established, and you may not enter [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]. The 5 NM core starts at the surface, so flying under the shelf to the core still enters Class C [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4a]].

steps.s: Next call: "N123AB, standby." What does that mean?
options: Communication is established; you may enter the Class C
You still need to hear "cleared into the Class Charlie"
Wait until ATC gives you a squawk code
You have been told to remain outside
steps.why: "(Call sign), standby" means radio communications have been established and you may enter the Class C [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]]. Class C needs contact, not a clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(1)]].

steps.s: Heading home, approach says: "Your ADS-B transmitter appears to be malfunctioning. Stop ADS-B transmissions." You wanted to climb to 10,500 ft MSL over flat terrain to top the haze, and your home route crosses the veil again. What do you do?
options: Climb anyway; ADS-B only matters in Class B and C
Comply, stay below 10,000 ft MSL, and ask ATC for an authorization before crossing the veil
Turn ADS-B back on after 5 minutes
Climb to 10,500; ATC knows, so you're authorized
steps.why: ATC uses that phrase for a faulty transmitter [[33:303|AIM 4-5-7d3]]. At and above 10,000 ft MSL (above 2,500 ft AGL) and in the veil, ADS-B Out is required unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]. For an inoperative unit, ask the facility with jurisdiction; that request may be made any time [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]].

final_quiz.q: You cruise VFR at 12,500 ft MSL over terrain at 3,000 ft MSL, outside Class B and C. What equipment does the airspace require?
options: None, since you are VFR in Class E
A transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out
ADS-B Out only
A transponder only
final_quiz.why: At and above 10,000 ft MSL over the 48 states, excluding at and below 2,500 ft AGL, both are required. You are 9,500 ft AGL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: You depart a nontowered satellite airport inside a Class C area. When must you contact the Class C facility?
options: Before engine start
Before takeoff, on the ground
As soon as practicable after departing
Only if you will leave the Class C
final_quiz.why: From a satellite airport without an operating tower, establish two-way radio communications with the Class C facility as soon as practicable after departing [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: A student pilot with the required 61.95 endorsements wants to land solo at a Class B primary airport that is not in Appendix D, section 4. Is that allowed?
options: Yes, with an ATC clearance
No, Class B always needs at least a private certificate
Only with an instructor on board
Only at night
final_quiz.why: 91.131(b)(1)(iv) allows a student pilot who has met 61.94 or 61.95; only the Appendix D, section 4 airports need at least a private certificate [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]] [[60:650|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 4]]. A clearance is still required [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You plan VFR at 17,500 ft MSL in Class E with a 978 MHz UAT ADS-B Out and a Mode C transponder. Is the ADS-B Out legal for that altitude?
options: No, UAT is allowed only below 10,000 ft MSL
No, you need 1090ES above 14,500 ft MSL
Yes, but only with an ATC authorization
Yes, UAT meets the rule below 18,000 ft MSL
final_quiz.why: Below 18,000 ft MSL, 91.225(b) accepts TSO-C154c or C154d (UAT) as well as 1090ES [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(b)]]. 1090ES is required only in Class A [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Before a flight into Class C, your transponder works but its altitude encoder has failed. When may you ask ATC for a deviation?
options: At least 1 hour before
Any time
At least 4 days before, in writing
You can't; the flight must be canceled
final_quiz.why: For an operating transponder without working Mode C altitude reporting, the request may be made at any time [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(d)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: A Piper J-3 Cub never certificated with an engine-driven electrical system flies 20 NM from an Appendix D, section 1 airport at 1,500 ft MSL, outside Class B and C and below the Class B ceiling. Legal without a transponder or ADS-B Out?
options: No, the veil applies to all aircraft
Only with an ATC authorization
Yes, under the no-electrical-system exception
Only during daylight
final_quiz.why: Aircraft not certificated with an engine-driven electrical system may operate in the veil outside Class A, B and C and below the Class B or C ceiling or 10,000 ft MSL, whichever is lower [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(3)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Arriving VFR at a Class D airport, your radio fails before you call the tower. What do you do?
options: Enter and land; VFR doesn't require a radio
Stay outside and divert; the conditions to land with a dead radio apply only once you are already in contact
Enter and land if the weather is at least basic VFR, you keep the tower in sight and you get a light signal clearance to land
Land at the nearest nontowered satellite inside the Class D without calling anyone
final_quiz.why: Under VFR with a radio failure, you may operate and land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower and you receive a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]], which is a steady green light without a radio [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

final_quiz.q: A part-time Class D airport's Chart Supplement entry says "other times CLASS E." The tower is closed. What is the surface area now?
options: Class G up to 1,200 ft AGL
Still Class D, without a tower
Class C
A Class E surface area, with no VFR radio requirement
final_quiz.why: When the tower is closed, a part-time Class D surface area becomes the class the Chart Supplement names, here Class E [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5a2]]. Class E has no VFR entry requirement [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6b]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has no ADS-B Out. En route outside ADS-B airspace, ATC tells you to climb to 10,500 ft MSL for traffic. What should you do?
options: Refuse; you can't enter ADS-B airspace
Climb, and advise ATC you are negative ADS-B equipment without authorization
Climb without saying anything; ATC cleared it
Ask ATC to file an ADS-B deviation for you later
final_quiz.why: Acknowledge and comply, but advise the controller you are not ADS-B equipped and have no authorization. The FAA normally won't take enforcement action when ATC started it [[33:304|AIM 4-5-7d4]].

final_quiz.q: You're at 9,500 ft MSL, 26 NM from LaGuardia (an Appendix D, section 1 airport), outside the Class B. Are you inside the Mode C veil?
options: Yes: within 30 NM and below 10,000 ft MSL
No: the veil ends at 20 NM
No: the veil ends at the Class B ceiling
Only if you are below 2,500 ft AGL
final_quiz.why: The veil is within 30 NM of each Appendix D, section 1 location, from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:647|14 CFR part 91 App. D, sec. 1]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: On a sectional, a magenta vignette on one side of a boundary means:
options: Class E begins at 1,200 ft AGL
Class C begins at the surface
Class E begins at 700 ft AGL
A Class D surface area
final_quiz.why: Controlled airspace floors of 700 ft above the ground are shown by a magenta vignette; a blue vignette shows floors other than 700 ft next to Class G [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]] [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6e]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly IFR through Class B. Besides the radio, transponder and ADS-B Out, what navigation equipment does 91.131 require?
options: An operable VOR or TACAN receiver, or a suitable RNAV system
An ILS receiver
DME
Nothing more for IFR
final_quiz.why: For IFR operation in Class B, the aircraft needs an operable VOR or TACAN receiver or an operable and suitable RNAV system [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(c)]].

final_quiz.q: You want to fly an airplane without a transponder in Class A. How must you request the deviation?
options: By radio, any time
Online, 1 to 24 hours before
In writing, at least 4 days before
At least 1 hour before, by phone
final_quiz.why: Requests for deviation from any provision of 91.135 must be submitted in writing at least 4 days before the operation [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(d)]].
